channel.title: High Impact News Daily
channel.description: The day's most important news, ranked by impact. No spin.

item.title: Morning Edition, Saturday, October 3, 2026
item.description:
The UAE attorney general said the Flydubai co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe in an attempted terrorist act. Counsellor Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said Saturday that investigators found the co-pilot on flight FZ1073 began carrying out a plan in the air, striking the captain in the flight deck with a crash axe and trying to take control of the aircraft. The Wednesday flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. He said the inquiry is still establishing motives, any links, and the physical and digital evidence, and that final results will come when that work is done. Flydubai had already said everyone on board was safe and had suspended Tel Aviv flights.

Five Russian air-attack weapons exploded in Moldova after crossing its airspace, President Maia Sandu said. Sandu said Saturday on X that she condemned the morning's attack on Ukraine and that five weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldovan airspace and exploded on its soil. Ukraine's air force said Moscow launched Banderol cruise missiles overnight at the Odesa region, which borders Moldova. In Kyiv, Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said a Russian strike damaged the Northern Bridge's road surface and trolleybus cables and suspended traffic; the Associated Press reported no casualties. Russia's Defense Ministry said it hit the bridge, claiming it is used to move troops and military cargo. Friday's attacks had already forced full or partial closures of three of Kyiv's six road bridges over the Dnipro.

French high-school protests disrupted 735 of about 3,700 schools Friday, with fires at school entrances and 1,747 arrests. The protests began in the Paris region in September and spread nationwide. Students say hours are too long, conditions are poor, including overheated classrooms, and too many staff are absent. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said 735 of about 3,700 schools were affected "in one way or another" on Friday, down 30 percent from Thursday, and that three staff members were injured Friday compared with 31 on Thursday. Since the movement began, he said, at least 65 staff have been injured, including 40 principals, about 170 students have been wounded, and more than 100 high schools have suffered severe damage. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said there were 1,747 arrests on Friday and that more than 300 police officers and gendarmes have been injured. An AFP photographer said fire damaged the entrances of two Paris high schools on Friday. The BBC, citing the regional government, reported more than €2 million in damage at Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes after a fire destroyed its glass entrance and some interior areas. In La Ciotat, officials said a teacher was sprayed with petrol and then assaulted. The Tours prosecutor said a young man injured Wednesday lost the use of his right eye. In Marseille on Thursday, police said hundreds of young people surrounded a fire truck at Saint-Exupery high school, forced the firefighters off it, and set the truck alight, Reuters reported. In Bordeaux on Sept. 29, Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas and academy rector Jean-Marc Huart said a firefighter was injured by an exploding aerosol can, according to press accounts, while putting out a barricade fire near Lycee Montaigne; he was taken to hospital and returned to his station that afternoon with several days off work. Unions and student groups called for further rallies on Tuesday.

A Miami federal judge dismissed a noncitizen-voting case, ruling the federal ban in 18 U.S.C. § 611 is unconstitutional; the Justice Department appealed. U.S. District Judge David S. Leibowitz ruled Thursday that Congress cannot set voter qualifications, a power he said belongs to the states, and dismissed the misdemeanor case against Chelsea Cox. CBS News reported the order applies only to Cox and is the first time a court has held the statute unconstitutional. It does not affect the separate law against false claims of citizenship. The Justice Department moved to appeal.

A crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman, the UK maritime office said. UK Maritime Trade Operations warning 149-26 said the master reported a port-side strike at 2142 UTC on Oct. 2. All crew were safe and no environmental impact was reported. Authorities are investigating. The report is separate from Friday morning's strike on an outbound tanker inside the Strait of Hormuz, which UKMTO said caused a small fire and a blackout before that ship continued.

The G7 agreed to a coordinated release of 100 million barrels, including diesel, starting immediately over four months. The leaders' statement, issued Oct. 2 after a virtual meeting, says the release runs through the International Energy Agency and includes a front-loaded substantial diesel release in the first 20 days. Members also agreed not to restrict energy exports to one another and asked the IEA for a follow-up report within 20 days, including on restocking. The statement condemns Iran's attacks and its disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and says sanctions on Russia stay in place.

U.S. employers added 29,000 jobs in September and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, the Labor Department reported. Nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000, well below economists' roughly 90,000 estimate. Private payrolls gained 46,000 while government employment fell 17,000. July was revised down by 31,000 to a loss of 10,000, and August down by 29,000 to a gain of 133,000 — 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported for the two months combined. Average hourly earnings rose 3.0% over the year to $37.81. The labor force participation rate was 61.8%.

U.S. stocks closed higher Friday after the soft September jobs report, with the S&P 500 up 0.7% and within 1% of its record. The Associated Press reported the S&P 500 rose 56.27 points to 7,722.72, the Dow rose 250.40 points, or 0.5%, to 51,176.96, and the Nasdaq rose 319.27 points, or 1.2%, to 27,190.86. Traders pared bets that the Federal Reserve will raise rates later this month. For the week the S&P 500 was still down 0.3% and the Dow down 1.3%.

Flydubai halted flights to Tel Aviv after a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight diverted to Saudi Arabia; the airline said all 172 people on board are safe. Chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said Friday that everyone on flight FZ1073 is safe and that captain Smit Machchhar is back in the UAE after medical clearance. The Wednesday flight diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said it suspended Tel Aviv service until further notice at the authorities' request, and Emirates suspended its codeshare on that route. The UAE attorney general ordered an investigation into the circumstances, motives and any terrorism link. The airline said that investigation should establish what happened on board.

A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations office said. UKMTO said the master reported a hit at 1122 GMT during an outbound transit. The strike caused a small fire and a blackout; the fire was extinguished and the vessel continued underway. No casualties or environmental impact were reported. The incident follows Tuesday's strikes on three Liberian-flagged tankers in the same waterway.

CDC declared over a multistate Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers that sickened 488 people in 34 states. As of Oct. 2, CDC said the Salmonella Javiana outbreak tied to fresh jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors is over. FDA closed its investigation the same day. Final counts: 488 illnesses, 65 hospitalizations and no deaths; illness onsets ran June 16 to Aug. 26. Traceback pointed to a common grower supplying Coast Citrus; recalled fresh jalapeños are past shelf life, though some longer-shelf products made with them remain on FDA's recall list.

UKMTO said the master reported a hit at 1122 GMT during an outbound transit. The strike caused a small fire and a blackout; the fire was extinguished and the vessel continued underway. No casualties or environmental impact were reported. The incident follows Tuesday's strikes on three Liberian-flagged tankers in the same waterway.

Russian aerial attacks forced the partial closure of three Kyiv bridges over the Dnipro River, the capital's mayor said. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said Russian strikes fully or partly closed three of Kyiv's six road bridges Friday, snarling traffic in what officials described as a new disruption tactic. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 100 drones overnight, including jet-powered models, hitting Kyiv and eight other regions; a drone strike on a Kyiv high-rise killed one person. The European Commission said it disbursed €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in the latest financing batch to Ukraine.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, October 2, 2026
item.description:
An executive order directs GSA to make America.gov the single online front door for major federal services. Executive Order 14432, signed Sept. 29 and published in the Federal Register on Oct. 2, tells the General Services Administration to run America.gov as a unified, Login.gov-authenticated entry point for public-facing federal services that serve more than 100,000 users a year online. Tax filing and Defense/Intelligence Community services are excluded. OMB has 90 days to issue an implementation memo; agencies must identify covered services and integrate them. In-person, phone, mail and agency sites remain available.

Homeland Security waived New Mexico water laws to speed border-barrier construction in the El Paso Sector. Secretary Markwayne Mullin's determination, effective Oct. 2, waives federal and New Mexico water statutes and related rules for barrier and road work from Border Monument 71 east to Monument 53, north to Monument 40, then east to Monument 1. DHS cited more than 1.24 million Border Patrol apprehensions in the sector from FY2021 through Aug. 30, 2026, and drug seizures including fentanyl. The waiver does not revoke prior Section 102 waivers.

The Pentagon is sending about 9,000 sailors and Marines and a third aircraft carrier toward the Middle East. A U.S. official told AP the move includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group with more than 7,000 sailors and about 2,000 Marines. With forces already there, the Navy presence could exceed 20,000 sailors and Marines and put three carriers in the region by late October. President Trump said new strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterms remain possible and that he rejected Iran's latest ceasefire and Hormuz proposal as inadequate.

Treasury and the IRS issued rules implementing the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit for K-12 school choice. Proposed and companion temporary regulations under IRC §25F (Education Freedom Tax Credit) allow individuals a nonrefundable credit of up to $1,700 a year ($3,400 joint) for cash gifts to eligible Scholarship Granting Organizations in participating states. Contributions may fund private-school tuition, tutoring, special-needs services, books and supplies starting Jan. 1, 2027. Thirty states have opted in; Treasury estimates ~96% of children in those states could be scholarship-eligible and projects up to about 2.2 million scholarships a year by 2030. Temporary rules set state election and SGO certification procedures now; taxpayers may rely on the proposed rules for 2027 contributions.

Federal Medicaid and CHIP funding ended for many refugees, asylees and other legal immigrants. Section 71109 of the 2025 Working Families Tax Cut law took effect Oct. 1, limiting federal Medicaid/CHIP matching funds mainly to U.S. citizens/nationals, lawful permanent residents, Cuban-Haitian entrants and COFA migrants. CMS told states to redetermine affected enrollees; KFF Health News found more than 281,000 people in nine states and D.C. at risk of losing coverage in October, with Florida alone identifying nearly 177,000. Emergency Medicaid for emergency conditions remains; states may still cover lawfully residing children and pregnant women under an existing option. Some states, including California, New York and Pennsylvania, are using state funds to blunt the cut.

Trump Accounts for eligible children begin automatic Treasury enrollment nationwide. Temporary IRS/Treasury regs (TD 10056), effective Sept. 30, say the Secretary will elect on or about Oct. 1, 2026, to create auto accounts for each child who meets age and Social Security-number rules and has no prior election—about 73 million eligible children. Auto accounts accept only Treasury-administered contributions and any $1,000 pilot payment until claimed; families then roll funds to a claimed or other trustee account. Regs also allow approved-class and publicly traded stock general funding contributions.

Treasury began mailing $500 Affordable Care Act refund checks to about 950,000 people in 30 states. The payments go mainly to HealthCare.gov enrollees who paid marketplace user fees and did not get federal premium subsidies, typically people above 400% of the federal poverty level; some unsubsidized people between 100% and 400% also qualify. The 30 states use the federal exchange rather than state-run marketplaces. Texas and Florida have the largest recipient counts. Checks began going out Wednesday with a letter from the president; delivery timing varies.

Cornell agreed to an independent review of its handling of a 2024 fraternity sexual-assault case as prosecutors reopen a charging look. After a September civil lawsuit and public backlash, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office is reexamining the case it declined to charge in 2024. On Thursday the accuser's attorney told NPR she told Cornell police in 2024 she was raped — contradicting the DA's Monday description of her statement; the DA said he had not yet obtained the full interview transcript from the university. Cornell confirmed it will bring in outside counsel for an independent probe, after Gov. Kathy Hochul called for a review. The university also edited a public FAQ that had said campus police shared all investigatory information with the DA's office.

A ~50-vehicle pileup on southbound I-95 over Lake Marion closed the corridor in South Carolina for an extended period. The morning crash near mile marker 100 on the Orangeburg/Clarendon County line involved about 50 vehicles, including roughly 15 tractor-trailers, South Carolina Highway Patrol and local outlets said. Dense fog was reported. About 11 people were hospitalized with minor injuries; the Clarendon County coroner said there were no deaths. Northbound lanes later reopened with slow traffic; southbound lanes stayed closed while crews cleared the bridge, with an SCDOT detour at mile marker 102. Officials urged drivers to avoid the area.

Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan's Helmand and Kunar provinces killed at least 10 civilians, Afghanistan and the U.N. said. The U.N. mission in Afghanistan said most of the dead were children and nine people were wounded. Pakistan's information ministry said the overnight strikes hit militant hideouts and that initial reports suggested 22 militants were killed; it did not immediately address civilian casualty reports. Afghanistan's Taliban government called the raids an act of aggression. The neighbors have traded cross-border fire for months over Pakistan's claims that militants operate from Afghan soil.

item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, October 1, 2026
item.description:
Tennessee halted scheduled executions after Christa Pike appeared still breathing following a lethal injection attempt. Witnesses said Pike still appeared to be breathing about an hour after pentobarbital was administered late Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville; she was taken to a hospital. Gov. Bill Lee ordered a third-party review and said the remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year. Earlier Wednesday the Supreme Court vacated a Sixth Circuit stay (Nelsen v. Pike, 26A428), clearing Tennessee to proceed before the warrant expired at midnight; Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissented. Pike, 50, was convicted of the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer and was the only woman on Tennessee's death row.

A State Department rule removed Syria from the blanket ban on U.S. defense-trade licenses. The International Traffic in Arms Regulations final rule, effective Oct. 1, takes Syria off ITAR §126.1's list of countries subject to a policy of denial for defense exports and imports. License requests will be reviewed case by case. The change follows the secretary's Aug. 19 defense-trade policy shift after statutory barriers, including terrorism-related restrictions, were lifted or waived. Belarus, Burma, China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Venezuela remain on the denial list.

USDA rewrote Rural Energy for America grants so projects must already be built before applicants can apply. The Rural Business-Cooperative Service final rule, published Oct. 1 and effective Oct. 16, shifts REAP renewable-energy and efficiency grants to a post-completion model using 12 months of actual performance data. It bars solar and wind systems on Farm Service Agency–certified cropland, bars components from foreign-adversary countries, limits applicants to highest-level owners, and replaces state contests with national scoring. Comments are due Nov. 2.

The Yankees, Padres and White Sox each swept their MLB Wild Card Series; the Phillies forced a Game 3. On Wednesday the Yankees beat the Red Sox 9-2, the White Sox beat the Astros 7-3 and the Padres beat the Cubs 4-1 to advance to the Division Series. The Phillies beat the Braves 4-3 in 10 innings, forcing a decisive Game 3 on Thursday.

The Senate confirmed Keith Sonderling as Labor secretary. The nomination was confirmed 47-41 on a party-line vote late Wednesday (roll call 256), with 12 senators not voting. Sonderling had been serving as acting labor secretary. The vote came after the Senate earlier Wednesday invoked cloture on the nomination 53-47.

The United States ended its anti-ISIS military mission in Iraq, withdrawing the last U.S. troops after more than two decades. Operation Inherent Resolve's Iraq mission concluded Wednesday under a 2024 Baghdad-Washington transition plan; roughly 2,500 remaining U.S. forces left, with Iraq assuming full responsibility for security against ISIS remnants. Iran and aligned groups cast the exit as a win. The U.S. and Iraq say they will shift to a bilateral security relationship; concerns remain about militia influence and residual ISIS threats without U.S. air and intelligence support on the ground.

A Flydubai pilot stabbed the other pilot on a Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight and apparently tried to crash the plane, Israel's prime minister said. Flight FZ1073 (Dubai to Tel Aviv) transmitted emergency codes including 7500 (unlawful interference), descended thousands of feet, and diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia; Israel scrambled warplanes amid hijacking fears. Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the Boeing 737; Flydubai confirmed a flight-deck altercation, said all passengers were safe, and said motives remain under investigation. Saudi airport officials said both pilots were hospitalized; Saudi and UAE authorities opened investigations.

Iran received a formal U.S. response to its proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the U.S. response to President Masoud Pezeshkian at Wednesday's cabinet meeting after receiving feedback via Qatari mediators in Doha on Tuesday night, officials said. The contents were not disclosed. A Reuters-briefed official said the main disagreement is the sequencing of a seven-day trust-building plan, not its components. President Trump had publicly rejected Iran's earlier offer days ago; mediators kept working. Pezeshkian said Iran would seek a "win-win" agreement.

The Ratepayer Protection Act and the Stop Insider Trading Act, both House-passed bills, failed in the Senate. Both needed 60 votes to advance and fell short the same afternoon. The Ratepayer Protection Act (vote 254, 57-43) would have pushed state utility regulators to keep large data-center power and water costs off residential ratepayers; four Democrats — Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff and Warnock — joined Republicans; the House had passed it 417-3. The Stop Insider Trading Act (vote 253, 53-47, party-line) would have barred members, spouses and dependent children from buying new publicly traded stocks while allowing sales with advance notice and letting them keep existing holdings. Separately, the Senate voted 53-47 to invoke cloture on Keith Sonderling’s nomination as Labor secretary (vote 255), clearing a procedural step toward a final confirmation vote.

Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight killed four people, including a child, and hit power infrastructure. President Zelenskyy said the main targets were energy infrastructure in Kyiv and the surrounding region. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed hits on a hydroelectric plant, a thermal plant, a substation, an energy storage facility and a data center; Ukrainian officials did not confirm those specific targets and reported hits on civilian areas in at least four Kyiv districts. Ukraine's air force said Russia is using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that are hard to intercept.

The Senate failed, 57-43, to invoke cloture on the Ratepayer Protection Act, stalling a House-passed bill on data-center electricity costs. Sixty votes were required (vote 254). Four Democrats — Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff and Warnock — joined Republicans; the House had passed the measure 417-3. The bill would have pushed state utility regulators to keep large data-center power and water costs off residential ratepayers. Lawmakers are heading into the midterm recess with the measure bottled up.

The Senate failed, 53-47, to invoke cloture on the Stop Insider Trading Act, blocking a House-passed ban on new stock buys by members of Congress. Sixty votes were required; the tally was party-line (vote 253). The bill would have barred members, spouses and dependent children from buying new publicly traded stocks while allowing sales with advance notice and letting them keep existing holdings. Separately, the Senate voted 53-47 to invoke cloture on Keith Sonderling's nomination as Labor secretary (vote 255), clearing a procedural step toward a final confirmation vote; post-cloture debate continues.

Armada Acquisition Corp. II shareholders approved the Evernorth XRP-treasury merger, a step toward a planned Nasdaq listing as XRPN. The noon-ET special meeting cleared the business-combination vote, according to meeting attendees reported by crypto.news; an official SEC 8-K with final tallies had not posted by evening research. Proxy materials project at least about 473 million XRP at closing if the deal closes. Approval is not the same as listing or trading — remaining closing conditions and Nasdaq requirements still apply, with completion targeted for late 2026.

OFAC published a final rule putting 2020 Iran sector sanctions into the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations, effective Sept. 30. The rule amends 31 CFR part 560 to implement Executive Order 13902, which authorizes blocking of persons operating in Iran's construction, mining, manufacturing or textiles sectors, among other authorities, and adds humanitarian and U.N. official-business exemptions. OFAC has already used E.O. 13902 for designations; this updates the Code of Federal Regulations. Willful violations may carry criminal penalties under IEEPA.

The Yankees, Braves, Padres and White Sox each won Game 1 of their MLB Wild Card Series on Tuesday. Yankees beat the Red Sox 9-0; Braves beat the Phillies 5-3; Padres beat the Cubs 8-0; White Sox beat the Astros 6-3. All four series are best-of-three; Game 2s are Wednesday. Teams that take a 1-0 lead have historically won the Wild Card Series about 88% of the time.

The Senate rejected, 47-51, a motion to force a floor vote on a resolution seeking a State Department report on Israel's human rights record. The motion would have discharged S.Res. 852, sponsored by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, from the Foreign Relations Committee under Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act. Sen. Rand Paul was the only Republican voting yes; Sen. John Fetterman was the only Democrat voting no. Sens. Cassidy and Sullivan did not vote. The Senate adjourned at 8:15 p.m.

The Transportation Department finalized lower fuel economy standards for new cars and light trucks. New vehicles must average 34.9 miles per gallon by model year 2031, down from about 50 mpg under the previous rules. The rule covers model years 2022 through 2031, ends the credit-trading program automakers use to meet the standards starting in 2028, and changes how vehicles are classified as cars or light trucks in 2030. The department estimates it lowers the average new-vehicle price by about $1,300. Environmental groups criticized the change.

A 100% Section 232 tariff on most patented drug imports took effect for companies not covered by the July phase-in. Under Proclamation 11020, the additional duties applied to Annex III companies from July 31 and to all other companies' patented pharmaceuticals and ingredients entered on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 29. Rates range from 0% to 100% depending on patent status, country, onshoring agreements and use; generics and many U.S.-origin products are excluded. Partner jurisdictions such as the U.K. can face 0%, and EU/Japan/South Korea/Switzerland/Liechtenstein patented articles face 15%.

The Supreme Court let the administration resume deporting immigrants to countries other than their own while the case continues. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson would have denied the request. The order pauses a Massachusetts federal judge's ruling, upheld by the 1st Circuit, that the policy denied immigrants a chance to raise fears of torture or persecution in the destination country. Deportations have included flights to El Salvador, Libya and South Sudan. The court will hear arguments in December, with a decision expected by summer 2027.

The Energy Department offered to exchange up to 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The request for proposal is the final tranche of the United States' 172-million-barrel contribution to a coordinated International Energy Agency release of about 400 million barrels after Middle East supply disruption. Crude would come from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with deliveries scheduled for November and December 2026; companies must return the oil plus premium barrels. Bids are due Oct. 6. Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged European countries to fulfill their release pledges.

Treasury sanctioned 10 people and companies it says procured weapons for Iran's Defense Ministry. Under Operation Economic Outcast, OFAC designated individuals and entities in Iran, Hong Kong, China, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey tied to procurement for Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics, including networks supplying electronics for drones and ballistic missiles. The action was taken under E.O. 13382. U.S.-linked assets of the designated persons are blocked.

item.title: Evening Edition, Tuesday, September 29, 2026
item.description:
The Education Department finalized a rule rescinding the Biden administration's 2024 Title IX regulations and restoring the 2020 rules; it was announced Sept. 28 and published Sept. 29. The 2024 rule, which had added gender identity protections and changed sexual misconduct procedures, was already struck down by a federal court. The restored rules govern how schools and colleges receiving federal funds investigate sexual harassment and misconduct complaints. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said the change matches court orders.

U.S. bans on imports of Canadian-bottled wine and spirits, whey and some motorcycles took effect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 29 under executive orders signed by President Trump. The banned goods totaled about $967 million in 2025 imports, and alcohol makes up 87% of that. The orders target Canadian provinces that pulled U.S. alcohol from store shelves. U.S.-Canada trade talks broke down in August; Ontario announced $1.15 billion in financing for affected businesses.

The Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act 77-22 on Sept. 28. The bill creates a federal right for college athletes to be paid for their name, image and likeness, requires schools to share media, ticket and sponsorship revenue, caps agent fees at 5%, and guarantees medical coverage for five years after eligibility ends. It now goes to the House.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, September 29, 2026
item.description:
President Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the war. Iran had offered terms to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil shipments, and end the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, now in its seventh month. Iran's foreign minister said Iran will wait for a formal U.S. response before abandoning ceasefire talks. Eight U.S. Marines were injured by an Iranian missile in the strait on Sept. 14.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.2% on Sept. 28, its highest level in 19 years, and U.S. crude oil rose 4.2% to $96.31 a barrel after President Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. All three major stock indexes closed lower: the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to 7,683.69, the Dow 0.67% and the Nasdaq 0.92%. Brent crude briefly traded above $108 before settling near $98. The 10-year yield is a benchmark for mortgage and other long-term loan rates.

President Trump announced at 2:00 p.m. that Mesabi Metallics, owned by India-based Essar Group, plans a $15 billion steel mill in eastern Iowa, using ore from its mine near Nashwauk, Minnesota. The mill would use iron ore from Mesabi Metallics' new mine near Nashwauk on Minnesota's Iron Range, which opened this month; the mine has hired over 200 of a planned 350 workers. Mesabi Metallics is owned by India-based Essar Group. No construction start date or mill job count was given.

Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi said Iran is waiting for an official U.S. response before ending ceasefire talks; an Iranian official said Iran will not change its position on its nuclear program. The statements followed the U.S. rejection of Iran's proposal. An Iranian army spokesman also said Iran's forces are prepared for renewed U.S. attacks.

SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time on its 14th test flight Monday, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The ship completed about six orbits over roughly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific west of Chile; the Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf shortly after launch. SpaceX changed the booster after ice buildup caused problems on the previous flight. NASA plans to use a modified Starship as the moon lander for its Artemis program.
